comments.name: Leila Piazza
comments.body:
I came to Phoenix, Arizona from Portland, Oregon to help my aging parents. I expected to be here 6 months based on my dad's poor health prognoses. That was 2.5 years ago. It was obvious my parents needed support to thrive as long as possible. My dad just passed on June 27. 

I don't like the weather and wouldn't have voluntarily moved here, but I love my parents. I'm glad I'm here. I helped my dad get off of a bunch of medications and his health improved significantly for over a year after I came. We made many happy memories.  

It hasn't always been easy and I've made a lot of sacrifices, but I did something so important for myself (that maybe not everyone is able to do). I kept some pretty strong boundaries around self-care. I didn't neglect doing things I love like hike with my dogs, make pottery, play my guitar, and work out. I spent time with friends, my boyfriend (who I met here with my dad!), and made time to go to Portland periodically to take care of my house there. 

I sold my home in Portland in April and that was a blessing. When my dad significantly deteriorated in May, I was able to devote my time and attention to meeting his needs. The last week of his life, dad was home with me, mom, my sister and our adult kids. He had the best possible situation in the end. Now mom and I will keep going, working it out one day at a time.

comments.name: M C
comments.body:
This video documentary was heartbreaking. My grandmother lived to 99 years old and her son who lived with her his entire life cared for her until she died. When she finally passed away, he was devastated. 

My family was lucky that my father passed away before he got to the point where he could not do basic activities of daily living for himself. He himself stated that if he were ever in that state he would prefer to die than continue with that low quality of life. 

My mother may need assistance someday, and we need to have that difficult conversation of who would take care of her and how. I have been very open and honest that I will not quit my job or put my life on hold to become a caregiver, and I think it is wildly unfair for anyone to be forced into this situation. 
1) Our culture does not respect the elderly to make this issue a priority to address. It fears death even more than aging, so that the goal in medicine has somehow become to keep people alive as long as possible regardless of their quality of life. We don't respect aging and we cannot tolerate death. 
2) Health care as a for-profit industry...nothing good can come of this.
3) Environmental toxins, processed foods, pollution, crime, poverty...these things all make health and wellness very difficult to establish and maintain. 
The issue with caregiving is complicated - cultural, political, economical - and will take a massive amount of change in multiple areas for anything to improve.

I recommend we do provide the best care we can for an initial phase in our own homes but we need to accept that the right thing to do is to place our old ones, after a time, in care faclities and then in hospice near the end.  This is realistic and the best pattern for the sick and the caregivers.

comments.name: E. Pluribus Unum
comments.body:
I could write a book about this.

I will spare readers most of it.

Instead, a happier story.

A lovely 60 year old Italian couple across the street with a large family and lots of grandkids.

The great grandmother had a stroke in her early 80s, and came home to die.  But she didn’t.  Although her weight dropped, despite good care, down to 80 pounds, and being bed-bound, she hung on.  Often jn a religious delirium, but half the time, fairly oriented, and happy with her daughter, grandkids, and great grandkids.  They adored her, helped care for her, and though all but one daughter had their own homes, the house was always full of people there seeing greadt-grandma.

After ten years, she finally passed peacefully with family around her.  

The family remained close.  But the house was never as full of life after great grandma passed.

I don’t need to be told that a large family is impossible for most people in 2026.  But one of the things lost now is having many willing hands and hearts to share caring for loved ones.

I have had psoriasis plaque on my body since I was 17 years old. Mostly my elbows, knees, and ankles. During eras of high stress and poor health (like mono and untreated autoimmune thyroid disease), plaque has also covered my scalp, inside my ears, my knuckles, my shins, and forearms. I had to quit playing fretted instruments because I couldn’t form calluses that wouldn’t perpetually scale off. My nails and fingers and toes looked geriatric by my late 30s. And full-blown psoriatic arthritis is a debilitating condition. 

At 62, a year into glp-1 treatment, I am six months into plaque-free living for the first time since 1980.   I haven’t picked up a guitar, I’m not tempting triggers, and scars and misshapen digits are forever. But this kind of essay is a deep threat to a wellbeing I thought I would never know again. 

I started to address a BMI of 29, a scale that wouldn’t budge despite the resources and information to eat healthy, but I’m staying for the anti-inflammatory properties that have markedly improved my quality of life with a lower side effect profile than before imaginable. My weight is now in the normal range exactly where I want it and after a half century of yo-yo’ing the same 50 lbs, it can stay. 

Quit vilifying an unimaginable leap forward in metabolic health with a low side effect profile. Instead focus on driving down cost and increasing access. Good lord, how do you have to be told? I knew the for-profit industry never actually cared about prevention.

The book is filled with useful suggestions on ways to enhance soil diversity, provide burrows, dead wood/organic matter, rocks, water, and other structures that can be used by wildlife for all purposes. Over the years I planted different types including many natives.  Even having two plants side by side, it was clear that the monarchs preferred that tropical milkweed and specifically in orange.  It was where you found their eggs and of course the caterpillars. Now that plant has a bad rap as it can spread EO, a bad and deadly pathogen.  That's mainly because it doesn't die back in winter in warm states/areas.  I learned how to keep it and keep the butterflies safe by not letting it seed, to cut it back yourself and dig up and treat the soil beneath it. Approaching ecological health from the perspective of relationships invites me to consider ecological restoration in a broader context. One of the most compelling ecological restoration writers of our time has launched a massive ecological restoration initiative that focuses as much on a system of exchanges of mutual gifts as it does on WHAT you plant.  She argues that such exchanges are the only way to mutual thriving. (Robin Wall Kimmerer, https://plantbabyplant.com/about/) This is worth highlighting! 

Also, there are networks of groups supporting micro-habitat restoration, with one of the most successful programs right in your home town! https://backyardhabitats.org/ This program, with more than 14,000 sites enrolled, emphasizes that micro-habitat is part of the solution, and connects participants to groups who are conducting the broader and large size landscape restoration that is needed to generate the scale of impact that we need. People might be interested to learn that there is even a group dedicated to helping more communities grow micro-habitat programs. https://www.villageandwilderness.org/. They are currently offering grants to help you get such programs established in more communities!

The Strip and Las Vegas proper away from the strip, yes people actually live lives there, has some fantastic food options.  The celebrity chef restaurants started by Jean Louis Pallidin leaving his Watergate restaurant in the mid 1990s started a remake of Las Vegas dining.  We go to eat, to see shows, to sit by a pool, and disconnect.  In the last twenty years, my wife and I have not thought to go to a buffet...maybe we should next time just to say goodbye to them.

They are thorough and systematic where he is ill-informed and impulsive. So they have managed to neutralize Trump's overwhelming power advantage.   Like many people struggling with obesity, I spent years trying different approaches. I learned that weight loss is not simply about willpower. It involves biology, metabolism, hormones, habits, stress, sleep, and countless other factors. For some of us, medications such as Zepbound help address the biological side of the equation in a way that diet and exercise alone could not.

 What has surprised me most is that the medication is not a magic solution. It is a tool. I still have to make better food choices, stay hydrated, remain active, and be mindful of long-term habits. The difference is that I no longer feel like I am fighting my own body every step of the way.

  Beyond the physical changes, I have noticed improvements in energy, mobility, confidence, and overall quality of life. Everyday tasks are easier, and I feel more motivated to continue improving my health.

  My journey is far from over, but going from 302 pounds to 264 pounds in seven weeks has shown me that meaningful change is possible.

I work in an industry that heavily depends on federal regulations.

It may sound paradoxical but businesses often like regulations.  The purpose of regulations is to publicize how the government interprets a statute that it is required by law to enforce.  Not having a regulation most definitely does not mean that the government cannot opt to not enforce the statute. Article II of the Constitution says otherwise.

This provides a more predictable business environment as businesses will generally know how a statute will be applied in specific factual situations.

The government has to interpret the meaning and intent of a statute regardless of whether it writes it down as a regulation. But regulations provide businesses knowledge in advance of the government's interpretation and that the statute will be applied in a uniform and predictable manner.

Throwing Trumpian chaos into this system is not at all helpful.

FWIW, here's my take on the surge of the far-right, and why the "do something" strategy as outlined in the article will not work.

The fundamental problem is that the standard of living of the "middle class" has been declining for 40 years, and this makes those people very unhappy.  At least in the US (I can't say for UK, FR, GER) the standard of living for the poor, and for the rich, has been *increasing*.   This is very visible, and further irritates the middle class.  The primary causes - automation, communication technology, and now AI - are only going to make these problems worse.

While immigration is not a primary driver of these economic changes, the reality is that humans are deeply tribal, and, if they are already irritated, going out and seeing a lot of people who don't look like them makes them even more irritated.

Finally, 90 years ago, government spending was 2% of GDP, so making some minor moves towards socialism (e.g. Social Security) could be made relatively cheaply.  Now with government spending well about 20% of GDP, getting taxed even more for income redistribution is politically not viable.

The far-right can't solve these problems any more than the center or the left.  They understand this, and their strategy is to give people someone to BLAME.  This is very comforting to the angry masses, even if in reality nothing is being done to fix things.

Heck, no one who spent ONE DAY AND ONE NIGHT walking around lower Manhattan and Brooklyn in 1990 would ever make that argument. 

NYC did not have the resources to direct-spend its way out of the crippling poverty, crime, and urban decay issues as they stood in the early 90s. And the federal government was not going to do it for them. We can sit around and imagine what 100s of billions of public dollars spent directly on poverty, crime mitigation, and public neighborhood reconstruction could have done and imagine how it would have made the city different as compared to the 100s of billions of private spending that actually occurred. After Hurricane Sandy I had to submit all paperwork to FEMA via fax. A tedious process. I was "awarded" a few thousand dollars to cover well over $10K worth of damage to my home. I was happy to get anything. Months later, I received a letter (regular mail) demanding the money back. Somewhere a mistake had been made and it needed to be rectified. I had to go through all the paperwork (again--and there was a lot of it) and resubmit my claim. Again via fax. An even more tedious process as the files had long been filed away and forgotten. After several weeks of anxiety, FEMA then sent another letter, simply stating that I was entitled to retain the funds originally granted to me. I was lucky enough to work somewhere that still had a fax machine in 2012/2013. I can only imagine how many people were unable to file a claim or dispute a rejected claim because they had no easy access to a fax machine. A FEMA representative once told me (over the phone) that over 90% of rejected Sandy-related claims were due to paperwork errors. These overhauls are needed and welcome, though I wouldn't trust A.I. to tell me the time, much less untangle federal/state/city red tape, of which there is enough to circle the globe more times than I can count. 
Let's be careful out there....

comments.body:
Some readers wonder why Le Pen is running for the 4th time when she has failed 3 times already. 

French politics work differently than the American version.

In France it is not unheard of to run and fail a couple of times before being elected President. Mitterrand was elected President on the *third* try (1965, 1974, 1981). Chirac as well (1981, 1988, 1995). They both went on to win reelection (Mitterrand in 1988 and Chirac in 2002). 

Legal problems aside, there is nothing strange about Le Pen running again. Especially since her party has gone from a fringe phenomenon to now being the most popular in France. Marine Le Pen herself has seen her score go up with every try: in 2012 she got 18% in the first round and was eliminated; in 2017 she got 21% in the first round and went on to get 34% in the second round; in 2022 she got 23% in the first round and 41.5% in the second round.  

Given this linear progression, her huge popularity, and historical precedent, she has every reason to believe she can clutch victory this time. Which obviously doesn't mean she will, but in her universe it makes sense to try again.

“She’s got far more political assets than Bardella,” Professor Marlière is quoted as saying. “ She’s been around for so long.” 

In fact,that's precisely her problem. Bardella is 30; Mme Le Pen will turn 58 next month. She indeed has been around for a long time, having become something of a shopworn figure in French politics. Sure, the RN faithful will vote for her. But they will vote for any RN flag-bearer, no matter who it is. 

But does Mme Le Pen have the wider appeal needed to win?  As an all-too-known quantity, she will have difficulty attracting votes from what the French call 'la droite fréquentable' -- 'the respectable right'.  In contrast, the pro-business, telegenic Bardella would very likely have had that broader appeal. 

In sum, Professor Marlière's view of Mme Le Pen's 'assets' is highly contestable. Her decision to run, thereby sidelining Bardella, is good news for all who fear an RN presidential victory.

I was surprised that neither the article nor the accompanying editorial perspective addressed the scientific and medical value of preserved hair samples. Such samples can contain genetic information that may help identify inherited disorders, disease risks, and other medically significant traits that could benefit Native American descendants through improved diagnosis, counseling, and treatment.

By not consulting medical researchers about the potential scientific value of these collections, The New York Times presented an incomplete discussion of the history, ethics, and possible utility of preserving hair samples. Readers would have been better served by a fuller examination of both the cultural concerns and the potential medical benefits.

comments.name: Jeanine Pfeiffer, PhD
comments.body:
While this article’s focus on the inclusion of hair samples taken from Native peoples as part of the hundreds of thousands of museum artifacts that remain at public and private museums is meritorious, most readers don’t understand the larger context: that it is **36 years** since NAGRPA (Native American Graves and Remains Repatriation Act) was passed, and only a portion of the artifacts have been legally returned to their closest descendants.

Every year that a museum delays repatriating items stolen from Natives is a year when more elders – who often are the only remaining knowledge-holders of critical cultural details about the artifacts — die, and the repatriation task for everyone becomes more difficult.

It is impossible to underestimate the profound grief and frustration felt by every one of the 575 federally-acknowledged Tribes and the hundreds of yet-to-be-acknowledged Tribal communities over these ongoing injustices.

Federally-recognized Tribes are allowed to consult for on the behalf of State-recognized or wholly unrecognized Tribes, but there is no such thing as an "Indigenous Group." That does not exist within the language or legal framework in which NAGPRA exists. That is also an affront to Tribal Sovereignty.

There is a difference between film music, which is heard in the background, and classical music, which needs to meet all its artistic strength with music alone. In an article in the most recent Weekend Magazine, the author made multiple references to "culturally relevant" music. How insulting to those who are devoting their lives to making great and serious art. But I suppose this is what the author meant: POPULAR music. Popular music is fine and entertaining and necessary. And I love a lot of it. But it is not the same as classical music, which seeks to make sophisticated narrative statements through sound. The US is in a long-term and pretty rapid cultural decline when it comes to many art forms, including classical music. The solution is not to continue to dumb things down. The solution is very simple: comprehensive music education and a national commitment to valuing serious art of all kinds. I wish I could read something in the NY Times that talked about serious musical art, but I can't. It's not "culturally relevant." Guess what? Life, especially in 2026, is way more complicated than this kind of music. Art is not made to "soothe" you!

Every structural steel project undergoes changes during the detailing process; erection and shop plans are the final finish product, not the Engineer's design drawings. 

It's a complex process where senior drafts-people submit questions to the Engineer regarding steel design plan discrepancies, and then the Engineer provides the solutions.  Then the shop detail drawings are submitted for approval - every beam, every column and brace detailed out with all the connections, welds and bolts. the Engineer reviews each drawing and stamps their approval or lists the required changes and requests the drawings be resubmitted before fabrication begins. 

Hard to believe, in this age of computer modeling and stress analysis, that they built a structural 3D engineering model from the original steel erection plans and shop details and suffered this kind of structural failure.

I had a background in appreciation of modern art as far back as a naive Stuyvesant H.S. student where MOMA's cafe was our candy store to hang out in after school. Can't explain it & never ran across many fellow Stuyvesantians there. Strictly a solo trip but I didn't mind. I even, dare I say, became a self-appointed docent when a group of people ended up in front of a painting: I was off to the races. (the level of ignorance of so many attendees was impressive - even younger ones who just wanted to be photographed in front of a canvas. ) Anyway, in my year at The Freshman Grad Division: an experimental program where the most naive students were given graduate faculty to see what the combination would produce - I ran across Marcia Tucker - as an art history lecturer and she ushered myself and other lucky acolytes into a deeper appreciation of classical art: all the greats - Botticelli,Titian,   Rembrandt (striking anecdote was how @ 62 he had married his 14 yr old maid - after he had lost his fame & fortune.). But we stayed in touch & became good friends. Really. So one day we were crossing Forty Deuce & the pavement was wet & reflecting the red & green traffic lights: Me: "So is that art?". She "Yes. Why not? What defines art or beauty for that matter?". And on and on. So it's interesting how that question (brought up here) lingers still. 
My question now is "But 'is it great?' e.g. banana peels. (Skeptical. Will it be worshipped 20 yrs from now?) 
Art Dir
Grt Am Play Series

Community members are so traumatized after many years of violence, occupation, and abandonment by their own government and the international community, that they have a hard time trusting the advice and actions of authorities - especially outsiders. What we are seeing in the Pacific is the ripple effect of a retreating U.S. hegemony and increasingly ambiguous commitments to allies that once placed complete trust in the alliance. Middle powers like Australia and Japan, which traditionally relied on U.S. security guarantees, are now losing their strategic orientation in a multipolar world. Fear and uncertainty naturally come first.

Australia, in particular, feels increasingly alone as the only major Anglo-Saxon nation in the region besides NZ. China is stepping into Australia's comfort zone simply because it now can. That doesn't mean China views Australia as a primary threat—far from it. Japan is a bit more concerning for Beijing, although the balance of power still heavily favors China.

China's growing presence in the Pacific is all about military expansion. I think the Chinese leadership has also learned from Japan's failure in World War II. Much of what we see today is deterrence-building aimed primarily at the US in prep for any move against TW. I don't think sending a few Australian or Japanese warships would fundamentally change China's calculations.

Australia needs to learn from its Asian neighbors and decide whether it sees itself primarily as an Asia-Pacific nation or an Anglo-Saxon nation. The same question applies to Japan. Pragmatism has long been the key to how Asian civilization states have coexisted for millennia, and that lesson may become increasingly relevant in the years ahead.

And in the case of the Antarctic Ice Sheet, regarding the marine based ice which is very sensitive to ocean temperatures—West Antarctica 3.3 meters of sea level rise equivalent of ice, East Antarctica 19 meters—we are committed to some response of the ice sheet to the heat that has already gone into the ocean. And Greenland has around 3 meters worth of marine based ice as well.

How much response? According to the paleoclimate record at 1.5-2°C above preindustrial temperature around 6-9 meters of sea level rise (we’re likely already committed to at least 2°C)
At 3°C, tens of meters eventually.

Times scales are the big question and the community in general has been conservative with time scales.
